newsitem.title: UK: Britain says Loyalist truce on, angering Sinn Fein.
newsitem.headline: Britain says Loyalist truce on, angering Sinn Fein.

text.p: Britain said on Monday that a shaky truce by Northern Ireland's Protestant "Loyalist" guerrillas was intact despite fears it had been ditched after an upsurge in violence by its Irish Republican Army (IRA) foes.

The IRA's political arm, Sinn Fein, angrily accused Britain of bias for refusing it talks while keeping up discussions with pro-British groups despite attacks and punishment beatings that bore the hallmarks of Loyalist extremists.
Even Protestant politicians admitted the Loyalist truce looked fragile.
"It does look as though the Loyalist ceasefire is crumbling," David Trimble, leader of the moderate Ulster Unionist Party, told Channel Four television in London.
But expelling "the political representatives" of the Loyalist guerrillas from peace talks would certainly bring an end to the ceasefire, he said, calling on the extremists to lay down their arms.
"Even at this late stage, I will say to the Loyalist paramilitaries and those who lead them, "Draw back, don't resume violence, because if you do, you're playing the IRA's game."
Sources close to the talks believe Loyalist parties have played a key role in keeping hardliners in check, and that expulsion could jeopardise their influence over the militants.

A statement by Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew that Loyalist militia were respecting a ceasefire was at odds with comments by the chief of police in the province that "Loyalist extremist groups" were behind two December attacks on Catholics that fuelled fears of a spiral of sectarian violence.

"I am very glad that the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC), so-called, has not moved back from the ceasefire which it announced 27 months ago," Mayhew said. "That distinguishes it from the IRA command which ended its ceasefire, evilly and quite unjustifiably, in February this year."
Two parties with links to outlawed groups in the CLMC guerrilla-controlling body have seats at the multi-party talks because the Loyalist ceasefire has operated since October 1994.
An informal session of the talks was held in Belfast on Monday and the next full plenary session is on January 27.
Britain says Sinn Fein will not be given a place at the table until its Irish Republican Army allies end an escalating armed campaign against rule from London.
The IRA, which wants to end British rule in Northern Ireland, abandoned a 17-month truce in February 1996 claiming London had reneged on a guarantee of a seat.
Recent IRA attacks dashed hopes of an early breakthrough to establish a new accommodation between Northern Ireland's pro-British Protestant majority and pro-Irish Catholics.
Violence has deepened the gloom surrounding the multi-party talks which have been plagued with difficulties since their launch last June.

"The refusal of Mr Mayhew to publicly acknowledge what is clearly evident to everyone -- that the loyalist ceasefire is over -- indicates the British government's determination to operate a policy of unilateral exclusion against Sinn Fein," party chairman Mitchel McLaughlin said in a statement.

The independent chairmen of the talks, former U.S.senator George Mitchell, former Finnish prime minister Harri Holkeri and General John de Chastelain of Canada, condemned the recent violence in a joint statement.
"We again urge those who look to violence or the threat of violence as a solution to political differences to set aside their arms and to engage in democratic dialogue."
